pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Add three one-digit numbers, using strategies including looking for a pair that makes 10 (e.g. 5 + 7 + 3 → 7 + 3 = 10, then 5 + 10 = 15). Ages 6–7, procedural application of associativity/commutativity plus bonds to 10.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y2 'add numbers using concrete objects, pictorial representations, and mentally, including... three one-digit numbers'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 2.OA.2 fluency and 1.OA.3 strategy use; 'add three whole numbers whose sum is less than or equal to 20' with make-ten grouping as the exemplar strategy.
• Operational details: the point is strategic grouping — scan the three addends for a bond to 10 (or a double), add that pair first, then add the third. Depends on quick recall of bonds to 10 and the freedom (commutative/associative) to reorder. Teach scanning explicitly rather than defaulting to left-to-right.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (age 6) — adds three one-digit numbers correctly by any method. Tier B (age 7) — for 5 + 7 + 3 chooses 7 + 3 first because it makes ten. Tier C (age 7+) — reliably scans any three addends for the most useful pair (ten or double) and explains the choice.
bestPractices: Teach an explicit 'scan for a pair that makes ten (or a double)' habit before adding.
Rehearse bonds to 10 to fluency so the make-ten pair is spotted instantly.
Use rearrangeable counters/tiles so children physically move the useful pair together.
Contrast a make-ten route with a left-to-right route on the same triple to show the efficiency gain.
Keep sums within 20 initially so the third addition crosses ten at most once.
keyRepresentations: Three movable number tiles that can be reordered
Ten-frame that fills to ten from the chosen pair, then takes the third
Empty number line with a jump to ten then on
Bonds-to-10 pairs chart as a scanning aid
commonMisconceptions: Always adding left-to-right and never scanning for a make-ten pair.
Not recognising a pair that makes ten because bonds to 10 aren't fluent.
Losing or double-counting the third addend after making ten.
Thinking the numbers must be added in the written order.
Miscounting when crossing ten while adding the third number by ones.

learn.summary: Teaches ages 6–7 to add three one-digit numbers efficiently by scanning for a pair that makes ten (or a double), adding that pair first, then adding on the third number — e.g. 5 + 7 + 3 → 7 + 3 = 10, then 5 + 10 = 15. The objective is the strategic habit of scanning and reordering (supported by commutativity/associativity and fluent bonds to 10), not merely getting a correct total. Includes a hands-on manipulative core, fluency/strategy-choice practice, a narration conversation, and a worked anchor, with each scaffold's role made explicit. Interactive and efficacy details are proposed, not validated.

activities.title: Drag a pair to make ten on the ten-frame
feedback: When a chosen pair makes exactly ten, the two tiles fuse into a '10' and the frame fills (e.g. with a glow/click) — immediate confirmation that these two tiles make exactly ten, the pair the make-ten strategy looks for.

When the triple contains a make-ten pair but the chosen pair does not make ten (it goes past ten, e.g. 5 + 7 = 12, or falls short), the frame does not land cleanly on ten, showing why that pairing is less tidy here. The total can still be found, just by a longer route. For triples built around a double (e.g. 6 + 6 + 3, which has no make-ten pair), the double is the useful pair even though it does not fill the frame to exactly ten, so do not mark it as less tidy.
A live-updating running total tile lets the child check the sum as each tile is added.
If the third addend is lost or double-counted, prompt: set the third tile aside and bring it in last, then recount.
activities.rationale: The target is a strategic move — scan, pair, regroup — so physically reordering tiles and seeing a pair snap to ten is intended to train the scanning habit and to make the regrouping concrete through handling. Live recolouring/overflow feedback is intended to show whether a chosen pair makes ten. These interactive details are illustrative of the mechanism, proposed and not validated or required implementations.
sourceClaims: Y2 pupils add three one-digit numbers using concrete, pictorial and mental methods.
Applying properties of operations as strategies (1.OA.3) includes grouping addends to make ten; 2.OA.2 targets fluency of such sums within 20.
Looking for pairs that make ten is a key mental-calculation strategy taught in early KS1.
learnerActions: Start with three movable number tiles above a ten-frame, e.g. 5, 7 and 3.
Scan the three tiles and decide which two you would add first: a pair that makes exactly ten, or, if there is no such pair, a double.
Drag two tiles together; if they make ten the frame fills completely and leaves a simpler 'ten and a bit' (here 5 + 10).
Deliberately try a less useful pairing first (e.g. 5 + 7 = 12) and notice the frame does not land on a clean ten, then find the better pair — it still gives a correct total, just by a slower route.
Repeat with triples that reward a make-ten pair, and with at least one triple that rewards a double instead.
Add the remaining third tile on last and read the running total.
activities.intendedInsight: Spotting the pair that makes ten (or a double) first turns an awkward three-number sum into an easier one: a make-ten pair leaves 'ten and a bit', and a double gives a known fact to add on to. The written order is not fixed, you are free to reorder, and any ordering still gives the same total.

activities.title: Which pair makes it easiest? — fluency and strategy choice
feedback: Confirm the efficient pair (e.g. 7 + 3) and point out that it is not the first two numbers written.
If the child selects the first two numbers by default, ask 'can you see two that make ten?' and rehearse the relevant bond.
Keep any timing light and supportive so it builds automaticity rather than anxiety.
activities.rationale: Practice with strategy-choice and quick retrieval is intended to build the automaticity that makes scanning easier. Recognition/selection items check whether the child chooses the efficient pair; they complement, but do not by themselves elicit, the hands-on reordering where the child freely moves the tiles and feels the ten form.
sourceClaims: Applying properties of operations as strategies (1.OA.3) includes grouping addends to make ten; 2.OA.2 targets fluency of such sums within 20.
Looking for pairs that make ten is a key mental-calculation strategy taught in early KS1.
learnerActions: Given a triple such as 5 + 7 + 3, choose which two numbers you would add first and say why.
Complete fill-in-the-blank totals for a set of triples, each containing a make-ten pair that is not the first two written.
Do a short, light timed set of spotting make-ten pairs to build quick recall of bonds to 10.
For each item, state the pair chosen and the leftover number before giving the total.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent recall of bonds to 10 lets you spot the useful pair quickly; deliberately choosing a make-ten pair can make the addition quicker and less error-prone than always adding left-to-right.

activities.title: Narrate the pair you chose
feedback: If the child narrates adding the first two written numbers every time, highlight the ten pair and rehearse the scan-first habit — the skill, not the concept, is what's missing.
If the child insists numbers must be added in written order, demonstrate that reordering keeps the total the same (any two may be added first).
When a pair makes ten but the third number is lost or doubled, bring the third number in last and recount.
activities.rationale: Narration can reveal the underlying strategy and prompt reflection on order and choice, though a conversation alone does not have the child physically handle and reorder the addends. Best used alongside doing and watching the procedure rather than as a substitute for hands-on practice.
learnerActions: A tutor poses triples such as 5 + 7 + 3, 8 + 2 + 6 and 4 + 9 + 1.
For each, work out the total and say which two numbers you added first and why that choice helps.
Answer follow-ups: 'Is there a pair here that makes exactly ten?', 'Would you get the same total in a different order?', 'For 4 + 9 + 1, which pair makes ten and which number is left to add on?'
activities.intendedInsight: Explaining the chosen pair makes the scanning strategy explicit and surfaces whether the child is truly scanning or just adding in written order.

activities.title: Worked anchor: see the make-ten pair highlighted
feedback: Point to the highlighted pair and the resulting 'ten and a bit' to anchor the method.
Note that this is an example to study: it shows the method but does not give feedback on the child's own attempts, so follow it with hands-on practice.
activities.rationale: A fixed worked example cannot be manipulated and gives no feedback on the learner's own pairings, but it can provide a useful reference model of the two-step strategy. Treat it as a scaffold that precedes, not replaces, active practice.
learnerActions: Study a worked triple, e.g. 5 + 7 + 3, with the 7 + 3 pair highlighted as it makes ten.
Follow the two steps: pair to ten (7 + 3 = 10), then add the third (5 + 10 = 15).
Describe in your own words how the pair was chosen before moving to practice items.
activities.intendedInsight: A clear model of the scan-pair-add sequence gives a reference point for the strategy before independent practice.

constraints: Keep sums within 20 initially so adding the third number crosses ten at most once.
Depends on quick recall of bonds to 10; rehearse these to fluency so the make-ten pair is spotted readily.
Offer triples where the make-ten pair is NOT the first two numbers written, so the task genuinely requires scanning and reordering.
Include some triples that reward a double rather than a ten, so the habit generalises to 'useful pair', not only 'exactly ten'.

Recognition/selection items (choosing which pair is easiest) check strategy choice but do not by themselves elicit the child freely reordering and feeling the ten form; pair them with hands-on or spoken production.
The worked example is a reference anchor only: it provides no feedback on the child's attempts.
Watch for losing or double-counting the third addend after making ten; bring it in last and recount rather than reteaching the whole strategy.
A correct total alone is not evidence of the strategy — ask which two were added first to distinguish scanning from left-to-right adding.
A less useful pairing (e.g. 5 + 7 first) still reaches the correct total; frame it as slower/less tidy, not as wrong.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and the interactive/efficacy details are untested.
Self-audit of arithmetic: 5+7+3=15, 8+2+6=16, 4+9+1=14 (matches the source answer key); make-ten pairs are 7+3, 8+2, 9+1 respectively — all consistent.
The claim that the make-ten route is 'faster and less error-prone' than left-to-right is taken from the row's discriminate note, not from independent empirical validation; it is kept qualified.

The source claim that '3D adds nothing' to adding three small numbers was removed as an unsupported categorical universal; the kept point is only that this task is planar/non-spatial, so a 3D model offers no particular affordance here.
One source (CCSS-M 1.OA.3/2.OA.2) and the NCETM guidance are marked verified:false in the row; treat their claims as unconfirmed.
The source describes timed/speeded retrieval; kept but framed as light and supportive to avoid implying speed pressure is required.
Pedagogy listed further representations (empty number line, bar/part-whole, bonds-to-10 chart) not developed into activities here; they remain legitimate scaffolds if elaborated.

probeDeeper: Which two did you add first, and why did you choose those?
Is there a pair here that makes exactly ten?
Would you get the same total if you added them in a different order?
For 4 + 9 + 1, which pair makes ten — and which number is left to add on?
assess.correctAnswer: 15, 16, 14. Watch for the child spotting and adding the make-ten pair first (7+3, then 8+2, then 9+1) and adding the remaining number on — rather than ploughing left-to-right.

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds strictly left-to-right, never scanning for a make-ten pair (5 + 7 = 12, then + 3).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Prompt 'can you see two that make ten?'; highlight bonds to 10 and rehearse the scan-first habit — the skill, not the concept, is missing.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Narrates adding the first two written numbers every time; ignores the ten pair.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'You have to add them in the order they're written' — refuses to reorder to pair the ten.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Remind that any two may be added first (associative/commutative); demonstrate reordering keeps the total.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Resists adding 7 + 3 first because 5 comes first on the page.

errorPatterns.pattern: Makes ten with a pair but then loses or double-counts the third addend.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Physically set the third tile aside and bring it in last; check the count. Don't reteach the strategy.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reaches ten then forgets to add the leftover number, or adds it twice.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot reliably total three one-digit numbers, or loses an addend when combining.
responseLevels.full: Scans the three addends, pairs the one that makes ten (or a double) first, adds the third on, and totals accurately and efficiently — explaining the choice.
responseLevels.partial: Totals correctly but always left-to-right, not spotting or using the make-ten pair.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Work these out, and each time tell me which two numbers you added first: 5 + 7 + 3; 8 + 2 + 6; 4 + 9 + 1.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Each triple contains an obvious make-ten pair that is NOT the first two numbers written. A child using the target strategy reorders to pair the ten; a child adding left-to-right can still get the totals but reveals no scanning, and is slower and more error-prone. Asking 'which two first?' exposes the strategy directly, so it discriminates even when totals are correct.
